TROUBLE BETWEEN COLORED PEOPLE AND POLICEMEN.
New York Sept. 27. An Atlanta Commercial
NEW YORK, Sept. 27.—An Atlanta, Ga., special in an evening paper states that during the commemoration services at DeGive's Opera House last evening the police keeping back the crowd were assaulted by a colored man, who was soon joined by others, and a general riot became iminent. Twenty-five thousand people lined the streets, and a panic at one time struck them. A scue of the wildest confusion ensued which resulted in the crushing of many children. [Special to the N. O. Democrat.]

ATLANTA, GA., September 26.—The largest crowd ever seen on the streets of Atlanta turned out this afternoon to witness the memorial services, under the auspices of Cœur De Lion, Commandery of the Knights Templar. At least thirty thousand people, more than half of them negroes, were congregated upon Marietta street, when the procession, the largest ever seen here, halted in front of Degire's Opera house where the funeral ceremonies were held. The procession was composed of the Commandery, the Fifth Artillery of the United States, the City Council, a regiment of local military, a battalion of colored military, several lodges of colored Odd Fellows and many other local associations. The Opera House could not accommodate one-tenth of the people, so a large part of the procession remained in the street with the vast concourse during the exercises. The Opera House was beautifully dressed, the black cloth with which the stage and galleries was gracefully hung bearing handsomely worked and bold insignia of the order—a magnificent metallic case surmounted a catafalque in the centre of the stage and to the front in a semi-circle were ranged the principal officers of the stage and to the front in a semi-circle were ranged the principal officers of the lodge. The Fifth Artillery band furnished the music, and fine addresses were spoken by Capt. Henry Jackson and the Revs. D. W. Given and A. G. Thomas. Appropriate resolutions were read and the exercises were closed with the doxology led by the band and choir and joined in by the great audience. While the exercises were progressing up stairs, a colored Odd Fellow, who could not jam his way in, got mad and kicked over a stack of guns, whereupon a soldier of the Fifth Artillery clubbed him with his musket, the negro's friends rallied to him, when the police rushed in, and aided by the Fifth Artillery, prevented a riot. This incident demoralized the crowd, which broke in every direction amid the shrieks of women and the shouts of men. A few moments later a police captain tried to arrest an unruly negro man at the foot of the stairs, when he struck at the officer, missed him, and planted his fist full in the face of a white lady, knocking her flat; thereupon the officer clubbed him tearfully; the soldiers and citizens wounding several negroes in attempting to keep back the crowd. Many arrests were made, and just as the police were entering the station on Pryor street, a negro man threw a large rock, knocking a white man down, near the door, and a crowd of negroes, bent upon rescuing their friends, formed in a line about a square from the station, where they were harangued by a large negro who brandished a huge butcher knife in his right hand, and told them to "carve their way through." Mr. KELLY interposes a seeming denial against the statement of Col. GEORGE BLISS, who says that in 1878 he had dealings with the boss of Tammany.

EDGEFIELD COURTHOUSE, October 31.—Edgefield is in ashes. The business part of the town is totally destroyed, only three stores being left. The Tillman Hotel was consumed. There are not provisions enough left to last twenty-four hours. The office of the Chronicle newspaper was burned. The Advertiser building and property is safe. OUR COUSINS GERMAN

Handsomely Entertained by the Good Folks of Chicago.

CHICAGO, October 31.—The Von Steuben party got an early start this morning, and had a ride about the principal streets with the Mayor and some prominent citizens. At the formal reception and welcome, Mayor Harrison astonished the German visitors by delivering, with some fluency, a speech in their native tongue, the purport of which was that republics are usually ungrateful, yet the services of Baron Von Steuben to this country were so important that gratitude dwelt in the hearts and homes of the people, not only for him, but his descendants. Colonel Von Steuben replied briefly and aptly in German, and Walker Blaine made a brief speech in English in his behalf. At noon the distinguished guests went on Change, and were received with hearty cheers and hand-clapping. The President of the board, Mr. Rogers, welcomed them in a few words. Mayor Harrison and Walker Blaine responded in their behalf, and then the audience tried to draw out Lieutenant-General Sheridan who modestly shook his head, remarking sotto voce to the Mayor, that he would attempt no speech lest he make a bull and displease the bears, a remark which the Mayor repeated to the board, causing much merriment over the wit of the soldier. POLITICAL.

Cannon, of Utah, Declared to Be as Allion.

SALT LAKE, U. T., Oct. 31.—The suit brought by Campbell to annul Cannon's pretended certificate of naturalization was decided today by Chief-Justice Hunter. The Judge held that, on the statements of the complainant and the admissions of the defendant, the certificate of Cannon was void on its face; that the pretended naturalization was a nullity. Thus the court in which Cannon pretends to have been naturalized twenty-five years ago decides that he is an alien, and therefore that Gov. Murray was right in refusing to certify that he had been duly elected to Congress. It is not supposed here that the House of Representatives can fail to take notice of this action, or, indeed, to be governed by it, and thus it is regarded as virtually settling the contest for the Delegate's seat from Utah in favor of Campbell. The Liberal candidates and the Liberals of Utah like tired soldiers at the striking up of music or opening of fire in front, are plucking up new heart in consequence.

MUNCIE BURNS, a well-known St. Louis sneak-thief, burglar and general desperado, was shot and killed by an officer the other night while endeavoring to escape arrest.

The locomotive and six cars were thrown into the Susquehanna River, and the remainder completely wrecked. The body of Ellis Quet, engineer, was believed to be under the engine in the river. NINE prisoners escaped from the jail at Lebanon, Ky., on the 31st, passing out through the tunnel.

GEN. MERRIWETHER LEWIS CLARK, a soldier in the Blackhawk War, the Mexican War and the late civil war, died at his home in Frankfort, Ky., on the 28th, aged 77. The deceased served under Lee during the whole of the late war, holding the rank of General at its close.

The Kentucky authorities were informed some time ago that the James boys had taken up their quarters in Logan County and had planned the capture of a train on the Louisville & Nashville Railroad. A well armed posse were dispatched to the alleged rendezvous of the famous bandits, but no trace of them could be found.

CHARLES JONES, colored, who committed an indecent assault upon a respectable white married lady, was hanged by a mob near Spadra, Johnson County, Ark.

NEAR Bennettsville, Marlboro County, S. C., the wife of a planter named Smith was set upon and horribly maltreated by a negro while returning home from a neighbor's. Her husband pursued the brute and shot him dead in his tracks.

Her skull was fractured and she received other injuries which it was thought might prove fatal. Her assailant was captured and locked up, and the neighbors threatened to lynch him.

At Halifax, N. S., while Mrs. Bethane was attending to a stove her dress caught fire. She rolled herself on the floor, attempting to extinguish the flames. A child crawling toward her caught fire from the burning carpets. Both were burned to death.

A STEAM boiler connected with a threshing machine exploded at Marlville, N. Y., on the 28th. Frank Millman was killed and eight others injured. Millman was completely disembowled, and died in half an hour.

The steamer Calcutta foundered at sea during a gale. All on board, twenty-two persons, perished. The British ship Omba, from Victoria for Melbourne, foundered. All hands lost.

APACHES have made their appearance in Sonora, killing a family near Rancho Santa Cruz, beyond Magdalena, and running off stock. Gen. Ottero, in command of the troops, has sent a force to co-operate with American soldiers, who are supposed to be in pursuit of them.

SEVERAL Danville (Ill.) firemen are under arrest charged with incendiarism. There have been many mysterious fires there recently, and it is now confessed by one of the malefactors that they were kindled for the purpose of waking the authorities up to the necessity of having a paid fire department.

SAMUEL KENYON, a well-to-do farmer residing near Black River Falls, Wis., was shot down the other night while returning from the well with a pail of water. There is no clew to the assassin.

The Mayer & Bachman Brewery, Clifton, Staten Island, and a block of buildings burned on the 31st. Loss estimated at half a million dollars. The Schmitt & Glade Brewery, Chicago, went up in flames on the same day. Loss, $150,000.

One of the most atrocious murders ever recorded in the annals of crime has occurred near Week's Mills, China, a beautiful little village twelve miles from Augusta. For cold-blooded wickedness and apathetic indifference, the murderer will rank alongside any criminal whose foul deeds have made mankind shudder.

WHERE THE CRIME WAS COMMITTED.

A mile north of the village of Week's Mills is a story and a half farmhouse, with a long, low ell attached. Around it stand trees of evergreen, which were put there to protect the cellar from the fierce frosts of winter. A little above the house are two substantial looking barns, built at right angles with each other. By one of these barns is a huge pile of manure. The farmhouse was the residence of two families. In one side lived Mrs. Deborah Merrill, a woman 54 years of age, and her son Charles, a young man nearly 23 years old. The other side of the house was occupied by Mrs. Merrill's daughter, a Mrs. George Lilly. Mrs. Merrill's husband has been away all winter at work in the woods around Moosehead Lake. Mrs. Lilly's husband is employed at the Insane Hospital in Augusta as engineer. Although mother and daughter lived under the same roof, they had very little to do with one another, and a strong feeling of antipathy existed between the two. So high ran this feeling that last fall, when Mrs. Lilly was confined to her bed by childbirth,

HER MOTHER DID NOT VISIT HER.

The son Charles, who has lived with his mother this winter, doing the chores, etc., is a very bad boy, and is generally disliked in the community. He is an incorrigible thief, and has been arrested several times for stealing. Last fall he voted the green-back ticket, and his mother who was an ardent republican, turned him out of doors and told him in the future he must earn his own living. He left town in quest of employment but did not succeed very well in finding work. Finally, after his father went into the woods, his mother told him that he might come home and remain through the winter. The first of February he returned. The sting of being turned out of doors in this fall still rankled in his heart, and he

NURSED HIS VENGEANCE.

Mrs. Lilly heard frequent altercations between the two, and they spent considerable time in bickerings. The mother would remonstrate with the boy for his misdeeds, and he would return a sullen answer. On Saturday afternoon. February 19th, the daughter saw her mother and brother drive off in the direction of the "Mills," in a pung. They returned about four o'clock. Charles drove around to the barn, and left his mother standing in the yard. That was the last time Mrs. Lilly ever saw her mother alive.

The next morning, Sunday, she had occasion to go to the kitchen in the other part of the house. She noticed that the windows and doors were open, and detected the stench of burning flesh. One of the stove doors was slightly broken, and she saw through the chinks something that looked like a piece of meat sizzling on the ruddy coals. Her brother was down cellar picking over potatoes. Mrs. Lilly called out:

"CHARLIE, WHAT IS THAT WHICH SMELLS SO?"

He replied that he was cleaning out the stove. She knew that he was accustomed, during his mother's absence, to throw all the cold meat into the fire, as he disliked warmed-over food, and she thought nothing further of the occurrence. The next morning she asked her brother what had become of her mother, and he replied that he guessed she had gone to visit several sick families who lived in remote parts of the town, as she had

PUT ON HER BEST CLOTHES and left home the day before. The sister's anxiety was thus dispelled, and she supposed that everything was all right. Monday, the young man came to Augusta with a lbad of potatoes. He returned home at nightfall.

WORKING UP THE CASE.

Sunday morning was one of the most beautiful of the winter. The warm air and sunshine hinted eloquently of approaching spring. The church bells were ringing out their first peals, to call people to the worship of Him who came to bring peace and goodwill to earth, when Coroner Libby and a Journal reporter started for the scene of a tragedy, where all laws, humane and divine, had been violated. In an hour and a half they arrived at the residence of deputy sheriff Percival where Merrill was under arrest. The fellow was loafing about, in the charge of a keeper, the most unconcerned man in the village. The house was a mile beyond. Around it were gathered hundreds of country people, in a state of intense excitement. New discoveries had been made since daybreak. A pile of ashes had been found in the rear of the ell, in which were fragments of the human skull, a few hairpins, a few buttons from a woman's dress, and a few slight ornaments. In the stable an axe had been found with its blade covered with blood. Men were constantly bringing into the house, little things which went to make the proof of murder irrefutable. A shred of calico was found, which Mrs. Lilly identified as coming from her mother's apron. All these things were taken into the sitting room where the body had been burned, and carefully inspected by Coroner Libby, Dr. George E. Brickett of Augusta, Dr. G. J. Nelson of China, and others. The room where the examination of the re-remains was held, was low posted with three windows. On the floor was a rag carpet. The walls were covered with pictures, and, horrible mockery, above the fireplace hung the motto:

A TWENTY-FIVE YEARS OLD SON MURDERS HIS
MOTHER, MUTILATES AND BURNS HER BODY.
THE CONFESSION OF THE MURDERER.

[Special correspondence of the Journal.]
Our quiet little town has been thrown into a fever of excitement over one of the most horrible and fliendish murders ever perpetrated, and which for brutality, has, in this State, never been equaled—the murder of Mrs. Deborah Merrill by her son Charles Merrill.

On the direct road between Branch Mills and Weeks Mills, about one mile from the latter and four from the former place, are the farm and buildings of Abram Merrill. They are in good order and repairs and Abram, who is a hardworking, honest man, could have made an easy living had it not been for his son. He is, or has been this whiner, at work in a logging camp 35 miles above the foot of Moosehead Lake. His family consisted of his wife Deborah, his son Charles, who has not been at home regularly until within the last six weeks, his daughter Fanny and husband, Mr. Lilly, who have lived in the northern end of the house by themselves. Mr. Lilly has been at work in the Insane Hospital at Augusta; this has left the two women much of the time alone. They have not lived very peaceably together for a long time and were not on speaking terms.

Mrs. Merrill was what might be called a strong minded woman; she liked, in the language of one of our selectmen, "to rule the roost" and generally succeeded. She was a large woman weighing nearly 160 pounds and was about 55 years old. Charles and his mother had quarreled as far back as the Sept. election, when he came home to vote, she not wishing him to vote the Greenback ticket, and they have quarreled frequently since.

Mrs. Merrill was last seen alive by her neighbors one week ago Friday last. Sunday and every day till Thursday, Mr. Mignault, living one mile from the house, called after her to go and help nurse his wife, which she had promised to do, but he found her part of the house fastened each time. Friday Mr. Howland, the nearest neighbor, called in to see Fanny. He asked her if he had not better go down to Augusta and see if Mrs. Merrill might not be there with some relatives. "No," answered Mrs. Lilly, "if no use to go down there, she is murdered, and you had better get out a crew and search for her." But he did not until Saturday, when search was begun in earnest, and toward night they discovered a number of small human bones near the watering tub and some in a barrel of ashes, looking as though the flesh had been burned off them. They then examined the large old-fashioned fireplace in the kitchen and found a very disagreeable odor of cooked meat. It was then too late to search further that night, and as suspicion pointed very strongly to Charles he was taken into custody by Deputy Sheriff Frank Percival and kept under surveillance in Percival's store at Weeks' Mills through the night. A guard was also placed over the house. Sunday, coroner Henry Libby of Augusta and others came up, and as there was little doubt that Chas. did the deed, Mr. Libby urged him to confess, but he would not. He finally called Mr. Percival one side and asked him what he had better do. Mr. Percival told him that if he did it he had better confess at once, which he did. Previous to the confession, however, the searchers had found more bones, also some hairpins in the barnyard and the bone of a leg minus the foot and ankle, with some flesh adhering to the same, all blackened and cooked. They found this in the manure pile back of the barn, which is situated about five rods to the north of the house. Chas. said that he and his mother had had trouble for some time that culminated on Saturday night, the 19th of February, at about 6 o'clock. He wanted the team to use awhile and went to the barn to take it. Mrs. Merrill came out and tried to stop him; he grabbed a hammer and struck her on the head, killing her instantly. He then covered the body with hay and went to the house. Sunday morning the neighbors, George Jackson and others, say that he went by their house-dressed in his mother's clothes and they thought at the time it was Deborah. Monday he took an axe and cut off the legs, arms and head from the body, which was frozen at that time and accounts for the absence of blood in the barn, cut them up in small pieces, carried them into the house and burned the flesh off in the fireplace, except that a little was left on one leg; he then hid them as before mentioned. Tuesday he cut the body into two pieces, put them in the pung, wrapped in a sack, and went down to Wind-or hoping to dispose of it on the way but there were too many teams-passing. He brought them home and deposited in the barn once more. Wednesday he took a load of potatoes and went to Augusta to sell them, taking the pieces on top of the load, wrapped up as before. On the road about five miles from the house are what is called the Barton woods, into which he carried them about five rods, made a hole in the snow, put them in and kicked some snow over them. He said his sister knew nothing of the murder, but people in the neighborhood think she did. They are very much against him and had they known of his confession before he was carried to Augusta, Sunday afternoon, he would doubtless have been lynched. Fanny, who has a young child, has been out very little this winter. She says she suspected nothing of the murder until Friday. She said there was a very strong smell of meat burning Monday and she knew her mother was not in the house, but Charles was always in the habit of stealing and she supposed he had brought something home and was cooking it up to get rid of it. She also saw him carrying the two pieces of the body into the barn when he came home from Wind-sor, and asked him if it was something he had stolen and wanted to hide before his mother got home. He told her it was not, but she did not believe him. She is considerably older than Charles and it appears very strange that she should know no more about it than she pretends, for Charles and his mother had to go by the windows of her end of the house in going to the barn that Saturday night, and Charles carried the head, arms and legs back to the house to burn them.

Charles is a quiet, modest appearing fellow, 25 years old but books younger, light complexioned, about 5 feet 8 inches tall, is not very tall and is a little round shouldered; he does not drink, use tobacco, nor swear, but has always had a bad name for thievery. He can probably keep as innocent looking countenance as any man in the state; hardly ever smiles or laughs and has not associated infinitely with any persons. Charles Merrill, the murderer of his mother in China, confesses the murder in all its horrible details. He is about 23 years old and has had a bad reputation for some time, having been frequently arrested for stealing. Last fall his mother turned him out of the house on account of his irregularities and he now confesses that he contemplated killing her at that time. There is a bill now before the Legislature for the re-establishment of capitel punishment and it seems as if a crime like the present ought to convince our legislators that the present law does not provide a suitable punishment. At a few minutes before nine in the evening a fire broke out in St. Patrick's Orphanage, at Scranton, Pa., and fourteen boys and three girls, ranging in age from six to twelve years, were suffocated. The orphanage was in charge of several sisters of charity, who had care of twenty-two girls and eighteen boys. The children slept on the third floor, a partition separating the dormitories. At 8:30 o'clock in the evening one of the sisters saw the children put in bed and locked the doors. She had hardly descended the stairs when she saw a dense cloud of smoke issuing from the rooms on one of the upper floors. Hurrying back to the apartment occupied by the girls she took one of the smallest in her arms, and the rest quietly followed her to a place of safety. By this time the fire was raging fiercely on the third floor, and smoke poured into the hallway. The sister who discovered the flames again began to ascend the stairs, but was told by a man whom she met half way up that the boys had all been safely removed. Four fire companies came on the scene in quick succession, and the work of combatting the flames was actively begun. In a short time the fire raging in the hallway was extinguished, and the firemen were enabled to reach the dormitory occupied by the boys. The door was battered in, and the discovery was made that not a single occupant of the room had escaped. The little ones were huddled together beneath their cots, many of them being covered by the bed-clothing. Not one showed a sign of life, and they must have been suffocated soon after the fire broke out.

THE WOMAN SUFFRAGE CONVENTION IN PORTLAND.

The woman suffrage convention in Portland Tuesday, May 10th, was called to order by Mrs. C. A. Quimby, of Augusta. Remarks were made by Hon. Benj. Kingsbury, Jr., of Portland, and Burton Firman, jr., a senior of Harvard College, for woman suffrage. Lucy Stone followed in her usual eloquent style. She began by comparing the present movement in favor of woman suffrage to the anti-slavery agitation. It is equally as important, she said, that woman should have the ballot as that the negro should. All just governments rest upon the consent of the governed. The governed consist not only of men, but of women. This government, in order to be democratic in the truest sense of the term, must rest upon the consent of women as well as men. She dwelt at length upon the position in which woman is placed by not being allowed to vote. She is placed in the same category with felons and paupers. Jefferson Davis is deprived of the ballot because he drew his sword against the nation's life, in other words he is reduced to the level of woman. After all the suffering we endured during the terrible days of the war, this great government refuses us the ballot, and gives the conquered rebel more rights than us. Mrs. Stone dwelt upon the success of woman suffrage in Wyoming Territory, also in England where women can vote in municipal elections. She asserted the need of women on health and school boards.

Miss Mary F. Eastman spoke next. She said this is not a question of expedition but one of justice. Nothing can be expedient which is unjust. We claim the ballot not as a privilege, but as a right. The woman who, prescribed as she is by the laws, says she has all the rights she wants, is deserving of pity.

Miss Eastman spoke of the objection urged that woman was not competent to legislate, and says that such an argument had no foundation either in experience or common sense. It is, however, but natural for those who have the power to think that it inheres in them.

Rev. W. R. Alger delivered the concluding address. Mr. Alger presented in a scholarly logical and concise manner the principal arguments in favor of woman suffrage.

CONVICTION AND SENTENCE OF MERRILL THE MATRICE

The trial of Charles E. Merrill of China, for the murder of his mother in that town, on Saturday, February 19th, by striking her upon the head with an iron hammer, began in Augusta Tuesday May 10th. An immense crowd was in attendance. After a little delay the jury was empaired. A number of witnesses were introduced by the government and a large amount of circumstantial evidence was brought forth to show the guilt of the prisoner. The confession made by the accused to Coroner Libby was admitted as evidence. Wednesday the government witnesses were all heard and the council for the prisoner made his statement developing the line of defence to be pursued. The homicide is admitted but it will be contended that an altercation arose between Merrill and his mother in the barn, and that in the heat of passion he struck her and killed her, and that his crime is therefore only manslaughter. There was quite a sensation in the Court room when the counsel announced what the defence will be. The trial closed Thursday afternoon. The prisoner was put upon the stand in the foreroom and made a creditable appearance, but nothing could shake the overwhelming evidence of his guilt. The arguments by the counsel were unusually able, and at twenty minutes of six the case was given to the jury. They retired and in six minutes brought in a verdict of "Guilty of murder in the first degree." Judge Whitehouse did not pronounce sentence on the Merrill murder case Friday, as intended, as the counsel for the prisoner requested that he might be allowed until Saturday to look up the question of law, and decide whether to carry up the case on exceptions to the law term. Saturday Merrill was sentenced to hard labor in the State Prison for life.

The Augusta Journal says that Merrill, the matriicide, when Judge Whitehouse passed sentence upon him, manifested great anger. He had told confidents in the jail, that if his sentence was over ten years, they would never get him back to jail alive. Deputy Sheriff Jewell fastened the "twisters" around his right wrist so firmly that they cut almost into the flesh. Mr. Sewall, superintendent of the county buildings, took his left arm in a vice like grip. On the way to jail Merrill said: "Take the twisters off; they hurt." Mr. Jewell responded: "It won't last but a minute." Then the prisoner made a mighty effort to break away. But the cruel "twisters," by a sudden turn, cut into his wrist, and the agony was so excruciating that it took the courage out of the fellow, and he was safely got into his cell.

Referring to the gamblers who frequent Baldwin and Jacksonville, the Tallahassee Economist remarks: "The men of this class from whom the travelling public most suffer are, we believe, those having their headquarters at Baldwin, the point of intersection of the two railroads. At and from this point they ply their vocation, but little if at all deterred by the warning some time since received by them in the shape of a visitation from Judge Lynch, when one of their number was killed. The Economist thus soundly counsels the farmers: "It seems to us that farmers should by this time know what it means to make their corn and meat, and when they do this they can snap their fingers at money lenders and merchants. It is the only safety for the Southern planter, any other course will make him a slave. This truth has been demonstrated so often that we need not enlarge on it here. The farmers have the game in their own hands if they will play it right; and there is nothing detrimental to the merchant in this. NEWPORT ARK, September 1
NEWPORT, ARK., September 10.—About two o'clock this morning the jail at Jacksonport was surrounded by a large number of masked men in arms. The keys were demanded of Jailor Lankford, who attempted to run, but was fired upon and captured by the mob. His life was threatened and a rope placed around his neck, still he positively refused to surrender the keys.

The infuriated mob then fell upon the jail doors with hammers, chisels and bars, and in less than ten minutes an entrance was effected. Henry Allen, who stabbed J. E. Williams in Newport on the 7th inst., was dragged to a locust tree near by and hung.

Sheriff Lofton arrived in time to command the mob to disperse, urging that the prisoner was safe in lawful custody. But the sheriff was simply waived to one side, placed under heavy guard and not allowed to speak out.

The Circuit Court is now in session, and the citizens, generally, are greatly incensed at the ferocious deed. As to who the participants were, remains a mystery to the public. Williams is still in a serious condition.

Abe Barnes, a freighter residing at Kearney Junction, Nebraska, and engaged in the business of hauling freight, was comming towards Custer. When about 20 miles below here he was joined, on the road, by a man known to many of our old residents, as "Fly Specked Billy," a desperate character, an outlaw, and formerly connected with Lame Johnny, of infamous notoriety. Billy informed the train that he had just left a freight outfit, going from Deadwood to Sidney, and that that he desired to visit Custer. He was allowed to mess with the train, partly through fear and partly for the sake of old acquaintanceship. The bystanders prevented blows being struck at this time, although only one or two were acquainted with the dangerous character of the man. The coroner's jury, composed of Odo Reeder, A. T. Feay, and Tom Wheeler, viewed both bodies on Monday and elicited the following testimony, in the inquest held on the body of Abram Barnes.
J. P. Altafer sworn and testified: I have known Barnes four or five years. I saw the shooting. I do not know of any previous trouble between Barnes and the man called "Fly Specked Billy." Barnes was playing billiards with Mr. Teague. The man who did the shooting was flourishing his revolver around very carelessly. He went outside and fired two or three shots, then came inside and asked several men up to take a drink. He kept looking around as if watching some one, don't know who. He said: "Is there any body here I know." He went up to Mr. Barnes, caught him by the shoulder and shot him. Barnes reeled towards the door and said: "Oh, I am shot." He just after that said to me, "Perry, I am dead."

Doctor D. W. Flick being sworn testified that he was called to attend a man who had been shot. Found the man had received a mortal wound and was dying. The ball had entered about an inch above right nipple in a diagonal course, through the apex of right lung. Judged from the amount of hemorrhage it had cut off a section of the pulmonary artery. It was a gun-shot injury, or of a pistol of large size calibre. In answer to the jury witness said, there was no question but that the wound was mortal and caused the death of Mr. Barnes. H. Moore being sworn testified that he was present at the shooting of Abram Barnes, on the night of February 6th. Barnes was playing billiards. Saw a man flourishing a six-shooter. Tried to get up to him, with intention of silencing him one way or other, but he kept turning around so it was impossible to get up behind him. He dropped his six-shooter down on Mr. Summers, but

J. T. Teague being duly sworn stated that he had been acquainted with A. Barnes more than a year; was present at the shooting. Mr. Barnes and I went into the saloon to play a game of billiards. We had just commenced the game. "Fly Specked Billy" stepped up to Barnes, who was on the side of the table nearest the bar, took hold of his shoulder with his left hand and turned him around, at the same time bringing the revolver in his right hand down on him. The shot was fired immediately, the powder set fire to Barnes' clothes. I know of no trouble between Billy and Barnes which would have induced the shooting. I had only known Billy five days. He joined us about 18 miles below here as we were comming in. The shooting occurred about ten o'clock in the evening. Mr. Barnes had always borne an excellent reputation.

Geo. Palmer being duly sworn testified that he kept a billiard hall in Custer city; was present at the shooting of A. Barnes. I saw the man who did the shooting come into my place about ten o'clock; he snapped the pistol at several who were present. He then walked up to Barnes and seized him by the shoulder and shot him. He then tried to escape out of door but was caught and arrested at the door. The man who did the shooting appeared to be somewhat intoxicated. He had a forty-five calibre Colt's revolver in his hand with which the shooting was done. Mr. Barnes had been perfectly quiet while in my place.

L. Lawrence sworn and testified: I saw a man come into the billiard hall who flourished his revolver around, snapped it at Mr. Summers', then walked up to Mr. Barnes and shot him. Barnes ran around the stove, then fell on the floor where he soon died. I think the shot fired by the man called "Fly Specked Billy" was the cause of Barnes' death. I have known "Fly Specked Billy" occasionally since 1870, did not know what he was doing then, but it was generally supposed that he was stealing horses; he was known as a bad character.

W. W. Summers sworn and testified: The man who did the shooting came into the saloon where I was; he had a revolver in his hand. He asked everybody to come up and drink. He stepped up to the bar and pointing the revolver at Geo. Palmer, told him to set out his whiskey d—d quick. A SANGUINARY encounter is reported from Round Oak, Jones County, Ga. A young farmer named Jack Wm. Gray interfered with a negro dance and was fatally stabbed by three negro brothers, Bob, Henry and Aik Jackson. Gray fired into the brothers, killing all three, one dying on the spot, one before reaching the door, and the other a few hours later. Gray crawled out of the house and died on the steps.

The college faculty admit that such a body was received, but say the disease was detected before it was placed upon the dissecting-table. The college has been quarantined by the Board of Health.

SMALL-POX in its most virulent form prevails in the vicinity of McCauleyville and Fort Abercrombie, Dakota Territory, and is spreading rapidly. The disease seems to be singularly fatal, some victims dying within twenty-four hours of the attack. It is said that before death blood gushes from the ears, eyes and nose of the patients. These symptoms suggest that the disease is not simple small-pox, but is in the nature of the plague.

McCoy, a prominent politician of Bonhomme County, is supposed to be at the bottom of the fraud, and he has been arrested.

It is understood that the British Government has divided the disturbed portions of Ireland into five or six districts, each of which is to be under the supervision of a sort of magistrate, who will be able to act without previous superior sanction, and have entire control of troops and police, with a view to prompt action in the event of a disturbance. A DISPATCH from Augusta, Ga., 27th, says: Between 500 and 600 negroes from Edgefield County, South Carolina, passed through this city to-day on their way to Arkansas. They are under the leadership of a colored preacher named Hammond, who promised to have a chartered train waiting for them at Augusta, but failed to do so, and the party had to pay full rate to Atlanta. They say they found it too hard work to make a living in South Carolina, and determined to go elsewhere. Hammond went to Arkansas some time ago to examine the country, and on his return advised the negroes to go out there. It is expected 1,000 altogether will go.

Eson Bolin, his wife and four young children not long since emigrated from Stone County, Mo., to Benton County, Ark., taking up their residence at the village of Rogers. A few days ago Bolin was shot and killed while asleep in bed, and his wife was suspected of the murder, which she thereupon confessed, alleging as a justification therefor that he had frequently threatened her life, that he had murdered two men, was a horse-thief and a bad man generally. She was taken to Bentonville and lodged in jail to await trial, where after a few days' confinement she cut her throat from ear to ear, using for that purpose a knife which she had borrowed from the jailer for the ostensible purpose of ripping up a dress. Mrs. Bolin's maiden name was Johnson, and her mother, now Mrs. Gibson, and other relatives reside in Andrew County, Mo.

A SENSATIONAL episode in the Guiteau trial occurred on the 28th, when he was placed in the prisoner's dock, by order of the Court, on account of his persistent violation of order and decorum. In enforcing this decision Judge Cox said in effect that the extreme latitude hitherto permitted the prisoner had been for the purpose of affording the experts in court the fullest opportunity to judge of his mental and moral characteristics, and that the District-Attorney has expressly desired this freedom be granted the prisoner. The expert testimony being now about concluded, the Court said no further good could result from these unseen exhibitions of the prisoner, and he should therefore insist hereafter upon the orderly conduct of the case. Guiteau at first manifested the greatest renunciation to being removed to the prisoner's dock, promising to keep quiet if allowed to remain inside the bar. The order was, however, enforced, and the prisoner took his place in court for the first time as a common criminal.

Horrible.
One day last week one of the most horrible and outrageous affairs took place in the little village of Adairville, Ky.: Sambo Bailey, living about three miles from town, on the farm of Mr. Heck Hummers, went to Adairville. While there he took a drink or two of whiskey and got a little drunk, as he usually does when he goes to town. He attended to his business and started home. Mr. Allen Bell, an ex-Representative in the Tennessee Legislature, a big man in the church, who can pray louder and longer and jump up higher when praying than any other man we know of. Mr. Bell saw Sam Bailey when Sam was starting home, and remarked to him that if he didn't mind he would fall off his horse. Sambo said to Mr. Bell that it was none of his d—d business it he did fall off. He used some other indecent language at which Mr. Bell became offended, and satisfied his revengeful spirit by striking him (an eye witness says) one hundred lashes with his coat off. The whipping was done in the livery stable. Bell got Sam into the stable, and ordered every man out; but one remained, a respectable gentleman, who saw the whole affair. He describes it as

A HORRIBLE SIGHT.

He says he is willing to swear that Bell struck Sam one hundred lashes. There are marks on his person to show that he was whipped severely. One of his eyes is very nearly put out. The weapon used was a buggy whip.

There is considerable talk among the colored people about the affair, and almost every one, regardless of color or party, condemns the course of Bell as unlawful, ungentlemanly and unrefined.

On the other hand there are few old sor heads, full of prejudice and ignorance, who approve of Mr. Bell's course. They are not yet realized that tails Negro is free and equal before the law.—Commercial.

The colored men were armed, however, and drove the assailants off, but they promise to return with fire-arms to-night, when a bloody time may be expected, if the threat is carried out. Conservator.

George A. K. Pomeroy, of Seymour, has been arrested at the instance of Beharrel Encampment Lodge I. O. O. F., No. 107, on a charge of embezzling the funds of the Lodge while Secretary. George Waggoner, the first settler of Salt Creek township, and the oldest man in Jackson county, died a few days since of malarial fever, at the remarkable age of ninety-eight years. He was a man of great physical endurance, and until the illness which terminated in his death he was never sick a day in his life, never knew what it was to have headache, toothache or backache, never needed the attention of a physician, and never took a dose of medicine of any kind.

A girl at Tombstone, Arizona, told her father that she had been insulted by a Mexican boy, in a logging camp, and the friends of the girl went to the camp and compelled the Mexicans to whip the boy until he died. Subsequently the girl said her story was not true and that she had told it for fun.

Russell Schoonover, aged 22, was shot by Daniel Nicholas, aged 15, on the 1st inst. No cause is assigned for the act. Schoonover will die.

At Lick Run, O., on the 29th ult., Dick Williamson and two brothers named Scott and James Tipton quarreled, when Williamson shot Scott Tipton through the stomach and James Tipton through the shoulder. The Tiptons returned the fire, but failed to bring down their game. Scott Tipton will die.

The Capture of Taylor, the Murderer.
The capture of John Taylor, the murderer of Captain Fletcher, at Chattanooga, in February, which was noted by us yesterday, was effected through the excellent maneuverings of Sheriff H. J. Springfield, of Hamilton county, who is one of the most efficient officials in the State. He has been quietly working up the case all the while, and was not baffled in the least by the reports of Taylor's having gone to Texas, and other reports. He received information Tuesday of the exact whereabouts of the fugitive, and at once organized a posse of six assistants and left on the train.

Arriving at Loudon at 11 o'clock that night, they were joined by Loudon county's young and efficient Sheriff Joe D. Fou'e and three others, and put out for Taylor's retreat, which was at the home of Mr. Van Stowe, 13 miles north of Loudon, on the Clinch River. They reached the place about daylight, taking all by complete surprise, the man of the house having just risen from bed. Taylor was yet asleep, and unsuspecting. He first talked as though he would show fight, but soon realized the situation, and dropping his arms quietly surrendered. He exonorated the family from harboring him, saying he forced them to let him stay there, where he had been a week.

CAPTURE OF A MURDERER.
John Taylor, Who Killed Capt. Fletcher in Chattanooga,
Arrested in Roane County and Returned to the Scene of His Murder.
Arrested in Roane County and Returned to the Scene of His Murder.

Special dispatch to the Chronicle.

CHARLESTON, April 6.

The jailor of Chattanooga passed down on No. 1 to-day with Taylor, as a who murdered Fletcher. Taylor was caught near Kingston, Tenn.

W. L. McKNIGHT.

The above special telegram was received by us late Wednesday evening. In addition to it, we learned from Capt. Wm. Elmore, conductor of the train, which came up yesterday evening, that Taylor was in custody at Loudon as he passed there, awaiting the arrival of the west-bound train. He was captured about daylight yesterday morning on Poplar Creek, Roane county. We did not learn, however, who it was effected the capture.

It will be remembered that John Taylor, about the middle of February last, brutally murdered Capt. John Fletcher, and old steamboat man, at Chattanooga, about a trivial matter, and then escaped. Taylor was himself a steamboat man, whose home was in Roane county. He formerly fired an engine on the E. T., V. & G. Railroad. He was regarded as a desperate and dangerous man. It was first reported that he had gone to Roane county, then it was given out that he was in Texas. This was no doubt started by his friends to throw the officers off the track. A reward of $250 was offered by Governor Hawkins for the arrest of Taylor.

Sheriff and Deputy Sheriff of Hamilton County Killed.
Thursday afternoon, 14th inst., on the passenger train, there was enacted a bloody and terrible tragedy. Sheriff W. T. Cate and Deputy Sheriff John J. Conway, of Chattanooga, were taking to the Supreme Court at Knoxville three prisoners—John Taylor, under sentence of ten years for killing Captain John Fletcher, J. L. Carter, white, under sentence of seven years for being implicated in murder, and Ed. Bivens, colored, under sentence for robbery. The train was in charge of conductor N. J. Bell and Sam. Toms. We condense the accounts of this affair as published in the Knoxville daily, and give the main part below:

At Sweetwater two men boarded the train and took seats in the same car where the Sheriffs and the prisoners were seated. At Philadelphia the train stopped, and the two men got up and came towards the prisoners, and the first thing known the man who proved to have been Bob Taylor, the older brother of the prisoner, John, presented his pistol within about six inches of Conway's head and fired, the shot taking effect in the left temple and going through and through. He hardly breathed, but fell over, with his head behind Bivens, quivered and died. Upon hearing the shot, Sheriff Cate rose up, drew his pistol and fired at the rescuers. As soon as Conway was shot, Bob Taylor secured his keys and pistol, unlocked John Taylor's handcuffs and gave him the pistol. John then fired and shot Sheriff Cate, apparently in the lawless, which seemed to stagger him. The shot of Sheriff Cate wounded John Taylor slightly in the arm. Some say Cate was shot again, in the breast, but by whom it does not appear. A general stampede ensued. Sheriff Cate, it seems, got down on the platform, and was in the act of aiming his pistol at Bob Taylor, when two more shots were fired, and he fell quivering to the ground.

As soon as the shooting was over Bob Taylor and his brother Andy, and the rescued prisoner, John, presented their pistols to Capt. Bell and ordered him to move the train out from there at once or they would shoot him. Bob appeared anxious to shoot him any how, but John interceded and prevented it. The three brothers then went
train out from there at once or they would shoot him. Bob appeared anxious to shoot him any how, but John interceded and prevented it. The three brothers then went forward with their pistols and took possession of the engine. Loudon was the next station, and engineer Toms was ordered at the penalty of his life, to pass through there without slacking speed. No halt was made until the train reached Lenoir's, where it was ordered stopped. The three Taylors left the train there.

Carter secured the keys to the cuffs, came on in the coach to Knoxville and surrendered himself and Bivens to Sheriff Homer Gilmore, of Knox county, who took them to jail. Carter received a slight wound is the right ankle from one of the shots.

The Taylor brothers, especially the two older ones, are said to be on the daredevil, reckless order. John, who was the prisoner, killed Captain Fletcher, an old steamboat and river man, at Chattanooga, nearly two years ago. He made his escape and was afterwards captured by Sheriff Joe D. Foute, of London county, the deceased Conway, and others, in Roane county. After several trials and mistrials, at the last term of Court in Chattanooga, he was sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary, for manslaughter, but took an appeal, and his case would have come up before the Supreme Court at Knoxville last Friday.

Dr. Lenoir dressed John Taylor's wound, the brothers pointing their pistols at his head to hurry him up. At Lenoir's they took three horses, one belonging to J. H. Welcker, of London, one from Dr Foute, and one from Win Bussell. After leaving Lenoir's the Taylors went to Kingston, where they took a quantity of ammunition. Forces were organized and started in pursuit. There are a large number, probably several hundred well armed men after the desperadoes.

Gov. Hawkins has offered a reward of $1,500 for the apprehension of the Taylors, and Judge Rae, of Hamilton, has offered an additional reward of $1,500, or $500 each for the Taylors, dead or alive.

CHRISTMAS DIVERSIONS.
Two Negroes Killed and a Nymph Badly Bombarded.
While Christmas is generally acknowledged to be a season of good cheer and happy reunion—a time at which we forget past differences and all meet for thanksgiving and general rejoicing, there are those who seem to think that unless they do some desperate deed on that day they have not fully commemorated it. Last Saturday and Sunday's pleasure in Waco and surroundings was somewhat marred among the colored people and demimonde by acts of violence which add none to the credit and good standing of the participants and may get all concerned into serious trouble. The first scene of blood we heard of was the finding of the body of a negro on the railroad track near Reagan. What his name was we could not learn, but have been informed that two trains passed over him. It is further stated that he was seen to have a bundle of clothes and was known to have money, all of which was missing when the body was found. It is thought that he was killed by some unknown parties and his remains placed upon the track as a blind to cover their villainy. Following this news comes the announcement that two Waco members of the demi-monde enlivened Christmas and the holy Sabbath morning by indulging in an unusual discussion. It occurred at the apartments of Mabel Clark, on Jackson street, and Nellie Cunningham figures as the principal actress. Some time just before noon it appears she had taken morning drams enough to wake up all the meanness there was in those she had the night before, and having nothing else to do took a pistol and made an unprovoked assault on Mabel, who, being defenseless, had to stand and wait for her to empty the pistol, which, it is said, she did in brief order. After she had satisfied her shooting propensity she retired to her room and barred the doors. When the police arrived she refused them admission, and a complaint had to be made by Mabel before they felt they had proper authority to break into the house. In the meantime the police got in and secured her by strategy. She is now in the county jail. The other woman was not injured. At the time the woman did the shooting she is said to have been very drunk and no doubt had not the least knowledge of what she was doing. By the way of a wind up one Nath. Williams, as he is called, who is said to have manipulated cat-gut at the dollar store for the edification of callers, put out the light of another negro, Bob Graves, on the John Bedwell place, about five miles below town. It occurred, as we learn, about 3 o'clock Sunday evening. Particulars as to the cause are meager, and to a large extent unreliable. Some say that all the darkeyes were drunk. Williams himself, who was caught yesterday morning, states that Graves siped him in the face before shot him, and others were credited with having said they heard Williams say he was going to shoot him just to see him kick. A courier came to town after an officer and Deputy Sheriff George Oglesby at once went down and spent most of the night trailing him with the bloodhounds. He had a great deal of trouble getting on his trail after he crossed Tehuacana, but before daylight got the dogs in good chase. The negro, finding himself hotly pursued, at last returned to the scene of the killing and gave himself up. Sheriff Van Hall happened to be on the ground and conducted him to jail. Such scenes sadly mar the Christmms festivities and do not speak in good terms for the participants, though all sensible people will not blame communities for the acts of individuals on such occasions.

BLOODY WORK IN ORANGE
St. Louis, August 23. — The Republican's special from Houston, Texas, received last night, gives particulars of the bloody tragedies, which have occurred at Orange during the week past, and which have been previously mentioned. They have caused intense excitement along the line of the Texas & New Orleans railroad, and fears are entertained that something worse is to follow. The citizens of Orange have risen en masse and are determined to end the reign of lawlessness that has prevailed for the past month. The present condition of affairs grew out of a difficulty which occurred three weeks ago between O. L. Delano, a noted desperado, and a detective named Wood, in which Delano was seriously shot. Wood escaped, and Charles Delano, a brother of O. L., accused the sheriff, Geo. Michael, of aiding in the escape, and swore he would get even with him. With this view he concocted a plan to assassinate Michael, and was aided by Dug Harris and two negroes, Sam and Bob Saxon. The plan failed, but they succeeded in very seriously wounding the sheriff by leading him into an ambush. The citizens became greatly incensed at these proceedings, and 150 of them congregated, captured four of the negroes and shot them. Bob Saxon was also captured, and after extorting a confession from him, in which he reviewed the plot to kill the sheriff and gave much other information, he was hanged to a tree. Another negro was arrested and hanged, and Chas. Delano was captured and placed in jail. A hundred armed men scoured the neighboring swamps for others of the gang.

BLOODY WORK. Eight Texas Desperadoes Lynched.
HOUSTON, TEXAS, Aug. 23.—Eight desperadoes have been lynched at Orange. It was the comparatively sober act of an organized band of citizens who determined to rid the county of a murderous gang of outlaws. The immediate cause was an attack of the gang on Sheriff George Michel.

One of the gang, O. L. Delano, attempted to escape from jail and was shot by Deputy Wood. The rest of the gang went to jail and demanded that Wood be given up. The sheriff was overpowered, the jail searched, and Wood was not found. He had been removed to a safe place. The gang, believing they had been deceived by the sheriff, threatened the latter's life.

The jail guard was increased, and the gang made futile efforts to get at the sheriff. They then began a series of outrages intended to draw the sheriff out of the jail, so they could attack him. Yesterday four of them, Charles Delano and "Dug" Harris, White, and "Sam" and "Bob" Saxon, colored, made a sham fight, cleaned out the saloon and burned the building.

The sheriff started for them, and followed "Bob" Saxon into a trap behind a covered fence, when a volley was fired, and Michel fell wounded with buckshot in many places. He was covered with blood. The gang believed they had killed him, and fled. Michel is now unconscious, and at the jail he is believed to be dying. The whole town rose up; a public meeting was held, and it was unanimously voted to lynch the gang, and a committee of 150 was appointed for that purpose. Early this morning four of the negroes were caught and shot in a field without preliminaries.

Robert Garzon, a colored leader, was captured and a confession was demanded and refused. He was hung to a tree until he was unconscious, and then taken down and resuscitated and was stretched five times before he made a full confession. He was then hanged a sixth time until he was dead. Finding they were right as to the men they had hanged and shot, and of others whom they suspected, they captured Sam Saxon and Charles Delano and put them in jail.

After a consultation it was decided to hang them, and they were taken into the street. While ropes were being procured they attempted to escape, and were shot, and their bodies were left bleeding in the roadway. O. L. Delano was then brought out and formally tried by Judge Lynch. He was dragged down the road with a rope about his neck and hanged to a telegraph pole.

Sheriff Michael Shot.
Orange was brown into intense excitement Wednesday night by the shooting of George W. Michael, our brave and gallant sheriff; and the killing and hanging which followed as a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community. To give minute details of the affair is impossible at this writing, but below we present a brief and as accurate a statement as possible.

Shortly after dark, Sam. Saxon, colored, and two or three other negroes made an assault upon a white man, Gus Garvey, in the Sample Room Saloon, several shots being fired. It seems that Saxon had threatened to shoot Garvey early in the evening and that the latter had purchased a shot gun to defend himself, but from some cause did not use his gun successfully. No one was hurt by the shooting. Sheriff Michael and deputy Ferguson were close by and started immediately in pursuit of the negroes, being joined by three or four others. When the posse reached a point just beyond Mr. A. Gilmer's residence and near negro town, they ran suddenly upon the negroes, who, it appears, were lying in ambush, and in an instant the posse was fired into, a shotgun charge taking effect in Mr. Michael's right arm and side. The posse fired, shooting Sam Saxon and another negro down, the others escaping. It was then discovered that the sheriff was dangerously hurt; news to the effect reached town, and in five or ten minutes at least one hundred and fifty citizens were in arms and in pursuit of the negroes. They were excited, and believing at the time that the sheriff was mortally wounded, left no stone unturned to capture the whole gang. Their success manifested itself the next morning in the shape of Robert Saxon, a brother of Sam's, hanging to the large oak in front of D. Call & Son's store, two others killed and a number wounded. We should state just here that Sam Saxon, after the shooting at the saloon, ran with his crowd out towards negro town, where he was joined by a num-
some discoveries the next morning caused a suspicion that the whole affair was a deep laid plan to kill the sheriff and deputy, and warrants were issued for the arrest of several white men as the originators, one of them being Charlie Delano, who was promptly arrested and placed in jail. Several negroes were also arrested, as accessories, and jailed. The Rifles were called out early in the morning by Captain Norsworthy, and kept on duty all day guarding the prisoners. — [Orange (Texas) Tribune, Aug. 19.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A32:
The Rioting in Orange.
[Special Correspondence to the Galveston News, Aug. 22.]
The rioting in Orange still continues and the wildest excitement prevails. About 8 o'clock last night the Orange Rifles, considering everything quiet and there being no visible signs of any intended outbreak, disbanded and returned to their homes, leaving the jail unguarded. About one hour later an armed party of citizens surrounded the jail and demanded its surrender. Deputy Sheriff Rance Jett, who was in charge, seeing that it was useless to contend with the overpowering force yielded up the jail. The invaders at once entered and took out Sam Saxon, the ringleader of the negro desperados, and another negro, said to be an accomplice. Saxon is the negro who escaped after the affray last week, but was so closely pursued by his hunters that he came up on Sunday morning and gave himself up and was placed in the jail for safe-keeping. Upon being taken out of the jail by the mob, Saxon's courage failed him, and he dropped on his knees at the deputy sheriff's feet, and throwing his armis around Sheriff Jett's legs, implored God's mercy upon his soul. Recognizing that all hope was gone, and that they were to be killed, Saxon and the other negro became frantic in their efforts to escape, and their terrifying yells of "murder" could be heard at a great distance. The exasperated citizens endeavored to quiet them, but to no avail, and at once filled their bodies full of buckshot. A general stampede was made by the congregations of the various churches, which were at worship, and the ministers fled their churches without a benediction.

Some startling confessions were made by Saxon before his death. He testified that he had been paid by Charles Delano to steal a carload of cattle last fall from the Louisiana Western Railroad, and that a certain woman connected with the desperadoes had offered him $500 to burn the town, that the spoils of a plot to which she was a party, might be reaped by herself and confederates. He attempted to accomplish this end but failed, only succeeding in burning one house and store, last fall.

A trial of Charles Delano was to have taken place at 9 o'clock this morning, at which Judge Lynch was to preside, and it is probable that by this time his neck will have been broken. Many of his accomplices are still at large, including his four brothers-in-law, the Harrises, and Ol. Delano and two negroes, but they are being trailed down and will, in all probability, be captured and suffer the penalty inflicted by an enraged community.

The latest news from Orange is that Delano, on being admitted to bail, secured his bondsmen against loss, and left Orange county, with several of his male relatives, apparently forever. Everything is quiet at Orange now.

Terror's Reign in Texas Dispatch to the Globe-Democrat
HOUSTON, Texas, August 25.—A meeting of 300 of the leading colored people of Galveston yesterday, and which called attention to the bloody outrages perpetrated on negroes at Orange by an armed mob of white citizens, and denouncing Governor Roberts and the state government for declining to interfere, has aroused a still higher degree of public interest in the late wholesale lynching in this state. The Galveston News is the leading paper in Texas, and several days ago called upon the state government to interfere and stop this dreadful slaughter of human beings, who were utterly helpless in the hands of a mob; but Governor Roberts has remained utterly silent. The facts of the whole business are that for six years a feud has existed between two parties at Orange, one composed of citizens of the town and its young white men, and the other of male members of two or three leading families in the surrounding country—the Harrises and others. Chas. Delano, the alleged leader of the opposition party, is a white man of 35, and married into the Harris family. He is a stock raiser and cattle man, and his followers, called by the citizens of Orange his gang, include, besides his kinsmen, some eight or ten negroes, two of them named Robert and Sam Saxon, mulates, and reputed sons of one of the prominent white citizens of the vicinity. As stated in the dispatch, Bob Saxon was hung in Wednesday's riot of last week, and his brother Sam was shot dead by a mob last Sunday night. Latterly Charles Delano was regarded as the leader of the Saxon, or negro, party, and Sheriff Michael of that of the citizens, and for months past a difficulty was expected. All sorts of crimes have been laid to the charge of the Saxon party, among them the robbery of the express agent at Orange by two masked men, and a short time ago the theft of cattle. Of course the citizens' party only waited for a chance at their opponents, and got it, but in the riot last week, when Sheriff Michael was shot, it has not been established, as stated by Michael's party, that the Saxon party were the first to fire on him, or that there was an ambush of negroes waiting to assassinate the sheriff, as claimed. Mrs. Delano, whom Sam Saxon

charged with hiring him for $500 to burn the town, is a lady with spirit and influence enough with her relatives to stir up a movement for revenge in case her husband is hung, as has been threatened by the lynchers. It is not believed that the friends of the Saxons will let the matter rest, but the reign of terror now existing in Orange may change into a reign of assassination. Persons who saw the shooting of the two negro prisoners taken from the Orange jail on Sunday night, say it was most horrible and brutally. The cries of the poor wretches were pitiful as they clung to the knees of the officers for protection, in the face of a mob of thirty men, but they were shot down like dogs. Orange is now completely at the mercy of the mob, who hung one negro and shot four others to death without a semblance of a trial. Delano's friends assert he had nothing to do with inciting the negroes to fire at Sheriff Michael.

ODD SHIPMENTS BY EXPRESS.

Babies, Bears Snakes, and Other Queer Articles of Freight.

"Odd freight? Well, I should say we have," said R. F. Masters, one of the oldest clerks in the main office of the Adams express company, on Market street, as he twirled himself around on his high stool and faced an inquiring reporter yesterday afternoon. Mr. Masters talks with great volubility, and, as he has a habit of dropping many small words, his conversation was decidedly jerky. "Yes, we ship a little of everything, from diamonds to Chester white pigs and Limberg cheese. Remarkable thing about that cheese. Ever smell any? Rich, penetrating sort of fragrance, ain't it? Case burst in freight room last spring. Made every one sick. Two Irishmen tried to shovel it up. Smell nearly turned 'em inside out. Got a Dutchman, regular out-and-out eat-a-sandwich-in-a-minute sort of a fellow, from Bergmyer's saloon across the way, but he gave out in ten minutes. Only finished it with a box of deodorizer. Phew! They should charge double rates to ship such stuff," and the speaker elevated his nose as though a trace of the diabolical aroma still lingered in his nostrils.

"Two babies have come through this office, one from Chicago for New York and the other from Washington to this city. The men on this line made a great fuss when the Chicago young one was shipped. Telegraph operators all along the route sent dispatches ahead and crowds of people went to the depots to see the baby. Came all the way in the express cars. Had a hammock rigged up. New idea, you know, and messengers thought it was a kind of a joke, but they wouldn't like too much work of that kind. Baby's mother died in Chicago, father lived in New York; weighed forty-one pounds, I believe; cost about two dollars and a half to send it through. Philadelphia baby came along some time after. Both made their trip first-class, and seemed to enjoy things generally. Fed 'em on regular spoon victuals from hotels along the line. Ofted have dead folks shipped. Don't know why they should send them by express tho', 'Tain't likely ane one's going to walk off with a corpse. Yes, a man shipped three Short-horn cattle clean through to Nebraska about a month ago. Unless he got 'em for nothing, they must have cost him a power of money when he got them. Just think of a man expressing a whole deer carcass two or three thousand miles. About as sensible for a butcher to express a beef through from here to Camden. Last fall a lunatic sent a twelve hundred pound block of cedar from California to New York. That's nothing, however, for I see some one sent twenty barrels of mess pork to the Pottstown military camp by express, and the charges amounted to over $100. sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A39:
The End at Orange-A Lame and Impotent Conclusion.
Since our last record two other negroes were killed by the mob at Orange. One of them voluntarily give himself up, and the same day was murdered. Before his death he gave information most clearly criminating Delano, the white leader of the band, who was in jail, and certain white confederates of his, persons who on account their wealth had heretofore defied justice. The negro stated that the wife of one of them had offered him $500. to burn the town. Yet in the face of all this Delano was not only not lynched, not only not brought to prompt trial, but was actually admitted to bail in the sum of $2000. on his promise to leave the country. We copy the just comments from the Houston Post:
The unexpected clemency of the people in reference to Delano, a notorious criminal, excites surprise and severe comment. Negroes who surrendered were shot down, but the ring-leader of the band, for some unexplained reason, is permitted to give bond and to leave the country. It is true we are not exactly in a position to judge of the policy of this extraordinary action of the Orange people. It is probable that they have adopted this method of getting rid of a bad character with his family and accomplices as the most obvious and easy of execution. But, in doing so, it should be borne in mind that they have left themselves under a reproach of compounding felony and something even worse, immediately upon the heels of a passionate breach of the law in the summary execution of Saxon and his companion. This is unfortunate in the last degree. The exigency of the occasion, the turbulence and excitement of the people may possibly be plead in extenuation for the precipitate action in reference to the killing of the negroes, though they cannot justify the violence. But the deliberate interference with the procedure of justice in the case of Delano, who should have been indicted for larceny, arson and murder, and his being turned loose upon the general community with the accusation of these crimes accompanying him wherever he goes, is an act not only indefensible but monstrous. We do not see how the people of Orange can defend their action in the premises. To be sure, they may thereby make a short-cut to the peace and order they so much desire, but the method by which this desirable end is obtained is both an illegal and an unmanly one. Why should they discriminate between Saxon, the tool, and Delano, the instigator? Why should Orange rid herself of a criminal citizen at the expense of the people at large?

three-men-clarendon-county.A3:
A YOUNG WIFE MURDERED. SHOCKING TRAGEDY IN CLARENDON COUNTY, SOUTH CAROLINA.
The Victim Knocked Down by a Negro and her Head Severed with a Hoe in the Hands of a Negress—The Three Murderers Lynched

CHARLESTON, S. C., Dec. 11.—The News and Courier has received details of the murder of Mrs. Kennedy, in Clarendon County, and of the subsequent lynching of the three murderers. Last Sunday Mr. Thomas Kennedy, living near Salem, intending to visit Charleston, went over to his fathers' house, a short distance from his own, to ask his mother to stay with his wife during his absence. Mr. Kennedy's wife was formerly Miss Ada Wright of Darlington, and had been married about a year only. She was 19 or 20 years of age, intelligent, refined, and highly respected. When her husband went away she shut the door and sat by a window to write a letter to her mother, little dreaming of the fate that awaited her. As she sat there she saw in the yard Joe Barnes, a colored boy, about 16 years old, who had been employed by Mr. Kennedy the previous week, and she asked him to bring her an armful of wood. This boy had been induced by two negroes living close by—Vance Brandt and his sister Julia, aged respectively 18 and 15—to hang around the premises, and when Mr. Kennedy left the place to give the signal to Vance and Julia, who kept themselves concealed in a thiefet. This couple had heard of Mr. Kennedy's intention to visit Charleston, and thinking that he would have a good deal of money in the house, determined to get it.

When Joe turned to go for the wood he gave the signal, and soon met Vance coming into the yard. Vance asked him where Mrs. Kennedy was, and went immediately to the widow, and three times tried to get in, each time being shoved out by Mrs. Kennedy. Finding that he was determined to get in she opened the front door, ran through the yard, and was just going through the gate when Vance snatched up a hoe lying in the yard, overtook her at the gate, and knocked her down. She implored mercy, and told him she would give him all the money she had if he would only spare her life. He cursed her and said: "I've been waiting to kill you a long time." He then struck her two more blows, in attempting to avert which it is supposed her hand was broken. Just then Julia came up with another hoe and killed her.

When Mr. Kennedy returned, about three hours afterward, he found his wife lying outside the front gate, mutilated, cold, and stiff, her head almost severed in twain. That day a jury of inquest returned a verdict, "Murder in the highest degrees by unknown hands." Several colored persons were arrested on Monday, but no clue to their guilt being obtained, they were promptly released. On Tuesday the colored boy, Joe Barnes, was arrested. He showed so much confusion on being questioned as to his whereabouts on Sunday that only a few questions served to bring out his full confession, from which the above account is taken.

Vance and Julia denied having anything to do with the murder, but the clothes which they wore on Sunday were bloody, and the money and pistol of Mr. Kennedy, found in their possession, were also stained with blood. On being questioned about the blood upon their clothes, the woman said she had killed a chicken, and the man said he had killed some partridges. On cross-examination the bloody finger prints on the hoe handle corresponded precisely with those on the shawl worn by the woman on the day of the murder, which circumstance had as great weight to convict as the boy's testimony.

The horrible character of the murder awakened intense indignation in the neighborhood, and 150 white men and 50 negroes assembled to punish the murderers. A further examination established the truth of the confession of Barnes. The negroes begged the whites to permit them to take the prisoners and burn them alive. This was refused; but a vote was taken whether they should be jailed and await the court or be lynched. Only twenty-three voted to await the law, and it was determined to hang them to the tree nearest the scene of the crime. Halters were obtained and fastened to a limb of the tree, a cart was placed under the limb, and the prisoners ordered to mount. Just then Joe Barnes begged to be allowed to pray, and began by saying that he had never prayed before, and never expected to pray again. Nothing was said by either of the others, except a groan, and "Lord have mercy," from Vance. Handkerchiefs being tied over their faces, the cart was pushed away and the three were left hanging.
