THE CLARENDON OUTRACE AND
ITS SPEEDY PUNISHMENT.
Details of the Horrible Crime-Three Negroes, Instigated by Cupidity, Brutally Murder a Young and Harmless Lady - The Guilt Fully Proved - Hanged to the Nearest Tree.
[News and Courier.]

NEW ZION, December 9.—In the absence of a representative of your paper, and at the request of many citizens, both black and white, I send you herewith a full and true statement of the murder of Mrs. Kennedy, and the punishment of her assassins.

On Sunday last, the 5th instant, Mr. Thos. Kennedy, living near Salem, intending to visit Charleston, went over to his father's house a little after noon, a short distance from his own, to ask his mother to stay with his wife during his absence. Mr. Kennedy's wife was formerly Miss Ada Wright, of Darlington, had only been married about a year and expected soon to present to her husband the first pledge of their mutual love. She was a young lady only 19 or 20 years of age, intelligent and refined and highly respected by all who knew her. When her husband left she shut the door of the house and sat by a window to write a letter to her mother, little dreaming of the terrible fate that so soon awaited her. As she sat there she saw in the yard Joe Barnes, a colored boy about 16 years old, who had been employed by Mr. Kennedy the previous week, and suspecting no harm she asked him to bring her an armful of wood. This boy had been induced by two negroes living near by, Vance Brandt and his sister Julia, aged respectively 18 and 15, to hang around the premises, and when Mr. Kennedy left the place give a signal to Vance and Julia who kept themselves concealed in a thief. This couple had heard of Mr. Kennedy's intention to visit Charleston, and thinking that he would have a good deal of money in the house determined to break in and get it. When Joe turned to go for the wood he gave the signal and soon met Vance coming into the yard. Vance asked him where Mrs. Kennedy was, and went immediately to the window and three times tried to get in and three times he was shoved out by Mrs. Kennedy. Finding he was determined to get in she opened the front door, ran through the yard, and was just going through the gate when Vance snatched up a hoe lying in the yard, overtook her at the gate and knocked her down. She implored mercy and told him she would give him all the money she had if he would only spare her life. He cursed her and said, "It's been waiting to kill you a long time," and at that struck her two more blows, in attempting to avert which, it is supposed, her hand was broken. Just then Julia came up with another hoe and severed her head.

When Mr. Kennedy returned about three hours afterward he found his wife lying outside the front gate, mutilated, cold and stiff, her head almost severed in twain. The entire cranium was cut off from car to car, leaving the brains scattered around on the ground.

A jury of inquest being held, returned a verdict of "murder in the highest degree by unknown hands." Several colored persons were arrested on Monday; but no clue to their guilt being obtained, were promptly released. On Tuesday the colored boy, Joe Barnes, was arrested. He showed so much confusion on being questioned as to his whereabouts on Sunday that only a few questions served to bring out his full confession from which the above account is taken. Vance and Julia denied having anything to do with it, but the clothes which they wore on Sunday were very bloody, with small particles of brains upon them. The money and pistol of Mr. Kennedy found in their possessions were bloody, and on being questioned about the blood upon their clothes, the woman said she had killed a chicken and the man said he had killed some partridges. On close examination the bloody finger prints on the hoe handle corresponded precisely with those on the shawl worn by the woman on the ill-fated day, which circumstance had as great weight to convict her as the testimony of the boy.

As was natural the community became so enraged and infuriated that a crowd of citizens, numbering between two hundred and fifty and three hundred, both white and colored, after due deliberation decided to hang the murderers to the nearest tree in sight of the place where the murder was committed. After satisfactory examination, which fixed their guilt, ropes were adjusted to the nearest tree, a cart was pushed under the tree, and the prisoners ordered to mount. Just then Joe Barnes begged to be allowed to pray, and commenced by saying he had never prayed before, and never expected to pray again. Nothing was said by either of the others, except a groan and "Lord have mercy" from Vance. Handkerchiefs being tied over their faces, the cart was pushed away, and the trio were soon dangling in the air.

three-men-clarendon-county.A17:
A Woman Hanged by a Mob in Laurens County.
The habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes in this State has gone on constantly for several years, and without censure, but now we are glad to see that two or three journals of the State have had the manhood to denounce the recent hanging of the half-witted negro woman in Laurens county.—Abbeville Press and Banner.

The hanging of this woman by a mob can not be too severely condemned, and we trust the officers of the law in Laurens County will ferret out the guilty parties and have them punished according to the enormity of their crime. The zeal of our esteemed contemporary in this direction is to be commended, but when it accuses the people of the State of "the habit of lynching weak and defeseless negroes," we think it is going farther than the facts will justify. The only lynching in the State that we remember, up to the time of the lynching of this woman, was for the heinous offense of rape and murder. The first fiend who met the vengeance of an outraged community for rape, was John J. Moore, a white man in Spartanburg county. Then followed the lynching of three negroes in Clarendon county for the brutal murder of a white woman and plundering of the house, and the lynching of the two negro brutes at Prosperity for the outrage and murder of Miss Wertz.

The indiscrtminate charge of murder and lawlessness against our people is common with the Radical sheets of the North, but the Press and Banner is the first Democratic paper in the State, or the South, which has made a similar charge. It would have been better for the good reputation of our contemporary to have given the number of "weak and defenseless negroes" lynched, and the character of the offenses for which they were lynched. If it had persued this course and then given its unqualified condemnation of the persons who committed the deeds and the papers who commended them, there would have been some consistency in its course, but when it makes a wholesale charge against the people of the State without giving the number of "weak and defenseless" negroes lynched, and the character of their offenses, we think it is placing itself in a very unenviable position to say the least of it. No doubt its assertion will be copied by all the bloody shirt organs of the North, and quoted upon every political rostrom by Republican speakers, as the highest Democratic evidence that their charges against the white people of the South are true. Such reckless and unjust charges are calculated to do us more harm than the treachery of all the Mahonns in the South.

At Wood Haven, L. I., Mrs Richards, 60 years old, has eloped with one of her boarders, Conn Mulverhill, aged 18. The lady was one of the most influential members of the Presbyterian church in the place, and Mulverhill was employed as a night watchman.

It is rumored that Oliver J. Smith, nephew of the lately deceased Sol Smith, president of the Merchants' Savings, Loan & Trust company, Chicago, is a defaulter to that institution, with which he was identified, to the amount of $31,000, and that he has absconded.

At Troy, N. Y., Wednesday, Henry Daniels was sentenced to the penitentiary for six months for cruelty to a 14 year old child of a woman with whom he was living. The boy was an idiot and was kept caged up in a filthy room at Daniel's house.

A party overpowered the deputy sheriff at Grand Haven, Mich., Wednesday, and obtained the keys of the cell occupied by a murderer; but while they were inside the sheriff's wife locked the doors, rang the fire alarm bell, and brought to her and a party of citizens to frustrate the plans of the would-be avengers.

Mrs Anna Harper, colored, shot and killed her brother-in-law, Joseph B. Harper, in Rockbill Township, Pa., on the 9th of June. The coroner's jury found that the shooting was accidental and Mrs Harper was released, but upon the discovery of new testimony she has been rearrested in Philadelphia charged with murder.

Mrs Carrie E. Andrews, on whose testimony Dr W. S. Weeks of Lowell, was convicted of conspiracy and blackmail against L. W. Forbes, with whom Mrs Andrews was found in dubious relations, has confessed that her testimony was false and was given by command of her husband who wanted to force Weeks to furnish money to bail him on a charge of horse stealing.

At Philadelphia, Sunday, James Gourley, who has been living apart from his wife, Dora, for some time, entered her house through a window and found her in a room with Daniel Dougherty, and began shooting them both. Dougherty was shot twice in the shoulder, but not mortally wounded. Mrs Gourley received a bullet in the left breast, which the doctors have not yet been able to extract. Gourley was arrested.

Harriet Stone, aged 14 years, has been on trial at Elizabethtown, N.Y., charged with the murder of an infant left in her charge. She testified that she had been criminally assaulted by the father of the child which it was charged she had poisoned, and that the babe was murdered by its mother to furnish pretext for a criminal charge against the prisoner. The jury appeared to have believed her, for they brought in a verdict of acquittal, after being out only ten minutes.

Alvin Watson, residing alone in Parkman, near Bangor, Maine, was murdered, Sunday night. His body was not discovered until Monday morning, when it was found fifty feet from his house with a wound in the neck from a knife that severed the jugular vein. There were also several cuts on the hip and side. Byron Chadbourne, a mute, about 20 years old, has been arrested, and admits that he committed the deed. but gives no reasons for it.

The body of Rev Sidney M. Stray, who was expelled from the ministry by the presbytery at Glen Falls, N. Y., for shooting his wife, was found in the Missouri river at Kansas City, last Friday. Stray had resided in Leavenworth since last March, but receiving a letter that his wife's brother had started west with the avowed intention of shooting him, he left Leavenworth, changed his name, and coming to Kansas City, it is supposed he took to drink and then drowned himself.
